originalTitle: Australia news live: Duniam promises ‘humdinger’ immigration policy and urges Coalition not to ‘act like a government in exile’
content: There’s a manhunt underway in Victoria after an alleged axe attack, with three people seriously injured. Andrew Messenger has the details here: Natasha Stott Despoja to lead inquiry into sexual violence in military Former Democrats senator Natasha Stott Despoja, who has done a wealth of work with women and domestic violence, will lead an independent inquiry into sexual violence in the military. The royal commission into defence and veteran suicide found there was a “systemic issue” in the Australian defence force and recommended such an inquiry. Stott Despoja tells the ABC the issue was both systemic and underreported, possibly by more than 60%. She said the inquiry would likely report by the end of next year. She said: I’ll make sure that we do this in a way that is trauma informed, victim-centric, and people will have the wellbeing and the legal supports that they need. But I do acknowledge some people have told and retold their stories, and I do not underestimate the level of trauma involved in that. So I’m very conscious of making sure that victim-survivors are at the heart and the core of this inquiry and that they’re treated with the dignity and the respect that they deserve. Coalition supports compulsory superannuation: Taylor Angus Taylor has been asked about Pauline Hanson’s calls for people facing tough financial pressures to be able to access their retirement savings. Hanson argued earlier this month that in a cost-of-living crisis, it’s not right to force people to save for the future when they can’t make ends meet today. Taylor has told News24 the Coalition supports the superannuation guarantee rate of 12% and notes there are already rules allowing people in financial distress to access some of their savings. He said the Coalition had an “an open mind” on revisiting its policy to allow first homebuyers to access more of their retirement savings for a home deposit. That policy was put to voters at the 2025 election and is being considered again by the Coalition ahead of the next poll. Taylor said: The important point I would make at this point is that we need to cap immigration based on housing supply, get more houses built, slash the red tape in the construction industry. Taylor unconcerned about tobacco donations to Nationals Angus Taylor has told News24 the decision by the Nationals to take political donations from tobacco companies is a decision for the party. The Nationals are the only major party in Australia to still accept tobacco money. The Liberals stopped accepting tobacco donations in 2013, when Tony Abbott was opposition leader. Labor stopped taking tobacco donations in 2004. In 2024-25, the Nationals received $225,500 from two large manufacturers. British American Tobacco donated $55,000 to the Nationals in 2022-23 for the first time in more than a decade. A year later, it sent the party $88,000. Taylor said he wouldn’t discuss donations to the junior Coalition partner: That’s a matter for the National party. I’m not going to get into that,” he said. We’ve made this decision. What this is about is doing what’s right for Australia and Australians. The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, says the Coalition’s plan for an 80% cut to tobacco excise won’t cause an increase in smoking rates, telling News 24 the new policy idea will undermine the business model of organised crime. Asked if cheaper cigarettes will see more people take up smoking, Taylor said “the horse has already bolted on this”: The price is already around $15 or less for most smokers, and anyone can choose to buy that. You can walk into shops all over the country and and pay $10 or $15 to buy a pack of cigarettes now. You’ve got to recognise the reality here. This is funding organised crime. It will disrupt the business model. It will take the profits and the customers away from organised crime in this country. Hold the tech bros accountable, Daniel says Here is former Goldstein MP Zoe Daniel’s take on social media: she says a “digital duty of care must hold the tech bros accountable for the safety of the spaces that they have created”: [Legislation] could also include misinformation and disinformation. This would risk the usual culture war debate about free speech, while we blithely accept the changes to our culture and society that are being freely imposed by Mark Zuckerberg, Elon Musk and others. What we should be worried about is the sovereignty of the information landscape and the fact that we’re being controlled by the systems – not the other way around. The onus will be on social media companies to identify and mitigate risks on their platforms under the government’s proposed legislation, Insiders host David Speers says, and that legislation will be unveiled this week. He says it will cover illegal content including illegal pornography being made available to adults, and for kids there would be “around half a dozen additional areas of psychosocial harm and that includes content around body image and bullying”. He says: The companies would face hefty fines of more than $100m if they fail to restrict this content and as for algorithms – regular pop-up messages would be required, asking if users want to stick with the algorithm or only see people they’re following and see what they’re posting. The user would have the choice. Researchers and the eSafety commissioner would also be empowered to police the social media platforms by using what are called ‘sock puppets’ posing as children to monitor what is being fed to kids online. You can read the background to this legislation here: Insiders host David Speers asks Duniam about the opposition’s proposal to criminalise flag burning. Duniam says it’s a “good idea” and talks about American patriotism. He says the move would help with the immigration debate: One of the problems we have is ‘who are we?’, ‘who are we inviting you to be part of?’ If we stood up for who we are and were proud as a nation, we could get onboard and deal with issues that flow out of
